title: The Molecules of Life
hook: Almost everything in a living cell is built from just four families of large molecules — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
key_points: Life's big molecules fall into four classes: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
Most are built from small repeating units strung into long chains called polymers.
Each class has a job: fuel and structure, membranes and storage, machinery, and information.
All four are based on carbon, which bonds in four directions to form complex skeletons.
content_html: If you took a cell apart and sorted its molecules, most of the big ones would fall into just four bins: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. These are the macromolecules — "macro" because they are large, often built from hundreds or thousands of smaller pieces. Each family has a characteristic job, but all share one thing: a skeleton of carbon.
extra_html: As Khan Academy's introduction to macromolecules describes, three of the four classes are polymers — long chains assembled from small repeating units called monomers, the way a brick wall is built from bricks. Carbohydrates string together sugars for quick fuel and structure; nucleic acids like DNA and RNA chain up nucleotides to store information; proteins link amino acids into the cell's working machinery. Lipids, including fats and the molecules of every membrane, are the exception — they clump together rather than forming neat chains. What unites them all is carbon, an atom that bonds in four directions at once and so can build the elaborate backbones life requires.

related.title: Water and Life
related.hook: Life is built around a single small molecule — water. Its odd properties make it the stage on which almost all of biology happens.

related.title: Carbohydrates and Fats: Fuel and Storage
related.hook: Sugars give cells quick energy; fats pack energy away for the long haul. Two molecule families, two strategies for powering life.

related.title: Proteins: The Cell's Workhorses
related.hook: Strings of amino acids fold into intricate shapes that become almost every working machine in the cell — from enzymes to muscle.

flashcards.prompt: What are the four main classes of large biological molecules?
flashcards.back_html: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Together these four families make up most of the structures and machinery of every living cell.

flashcards.prompt: Many of life's large molecules are polymers. What does that mean?

choices.text: They are long chains built from many small repeating subunits
They are single atoms with no internal structure
They are always made of pure metal

flashcards.explanation_html: A polymer is a chain of many small units, called monomers, linked together — like beads on a string. Proteins, nucleic acids, and many carbohydrates are built this way.

flashcards.prompt: Which element forms the backbone of all four classes of biological molecules?
flashcards.explanation_html: Carbon can form four stable bonds, letting it build long chains, rings, and branches. That versatility makes it the structural core of life's molecules.
